slides.title: Agent engineering path – what you will find here
slides.subtitle: Short overview; details on later slides

sections.heading: In short
sections.body:
**MUST path:** agent cycle → 3A strategy → depth and roles → 5 workflow patterns → role and system prompt → tools → when to choose an agent → errors and limits → workflow concepts → automation platforms → launch.

**Optional:** GitHub, deeper spec, glossary, summary. Term definitions – on the **Key concepts** slide.

sections.heading: Quick win in 60 sec.
sections.body: Before deeper theory, do one small check: can you already tell an agent from a simple question–answer?

sections.heading: Copyable prompt
sections.body: Copy it into AI and adapt the example to your work.
sections.copyable: Explain in one sentence how an AI agent differs from a simple question–answer. Give one example from my work where an agent is needed, not a single simple prompt.

sections.heading: Check
sections.body: If the answer shows neither multiple steps nor tool use, it is still a simple prompt. On the next slide you will see the full agent cycle.

slides.title: Agent cycle and architecture
slides.subtitle: Agent → Planning → Tools → Environment → Result → Feedback

sections.heading: In short
sections.body: The diagram below – **five cycle steps**. Unlike in a simple chat, the agent **autonomously** chooses actions and can call tools.

sections.heading: How an AI agent works
sections.body: Click a step – explanation below. To view it full size, open the same image in the modal.

sections.heading: API and looping
sections.body:
**API** – a program’s “door” to data or actions: the agent calls your CRM, email or another system through it, because it does not “have” that data itself.

**Looping:** after the result the agent decides – repeat a step, call another tool, or finish. That is the feedback at the end of the cycle.

sections.heading: When to choose an agent
sections.body: More detail on when to use an agent instead of a simple prompt – with examples – on **When to choose an agent vs. a simple prompt**.

sections.heading: Do this now
sections.body: Apply the cycle to your process – copy the task into AI.

sections.heading: Copyable prompt
sections.body: Fill [DESCRIBE] with your work.
sections.copyable:
My process: [DESCRIBE, e.g. customer email sorting].
Walk the agent cycle: (1) what is the task, (2) what is the plan, (3) which tool you will call, (4) what environment / data you read, (5) what is the result and whether to loop.
In one sentence: where in this process is a tool required (not only a text answer)?

sections.heading: Check
sections.body: Can you show in your process **where the cycle calls a tool** and **where feedback** may repeat a step? If not – go back to the diagram.

content.title: Agent cycle – I ran 1 agent request
content.body: Run a short agent request with search or a tool. Mark this step when the answer shows not only text, but clear steps, sources, or a tool trace.

sections.heading: Check
sections.body: Does the answer have at least 2 steps? Does it say which tool the AI used – or why it used none?
sections.copyable: Task: [DESCRIBE]. Use search or a tool if needed. Return the answer in 3 steps: what you did, which tool you used, what the result is. If you used no tool – explain why.

sections.heading: If it fails
sections.body: Add sentences to the task: “use search”, “cite sources”, “if you cannot find it – write Not found”.

sections.heading: In short
sections.body: 3A is a **decision portfolio**, not “more agents = better”. Most work – rules (**fewer errors**, predictable); a smaller share – human + AI (judgment and ownership); the smallest – agents with limits (costly and risky). **80/15/5** protects speed and safety – it is not a maturity ladder to autopilot.

sections.heading: Three bands – when to choose
sections.body:
**Automate (80 %)** – what it is: rules that do not need a human at every step. Why: fewer errors, predictable. E.g., form → CRM → email.

**Augment (15 %)** – how much: human decides, AI helps. Why: ownership or context needed. E.g.: AI draft → human approves → send.

**Autonomize (5 %)** – how much: agent with limits and escalation. Why: narrow band – higher risk. E.g.: feedback → sentiment → escalate to a human.

sections.heading: 3A strategy (diagram)
sections.body: Click a band – when to choose. Then assign your processes below.

sections.heading: Example
sections.body: **Same process – two bands.** Customer email → reply: if a template reply (“received / ticket #”) is enough → **Automate**. If AI drafts the reply and a human approves the tone and facts → **Augment**. Choose Autonomize only with clear limits and escalation.

sections.heading: Do this now
sections.body: List **three of your work processes** and assign each to one 3A band. Copy the template into AI or write it down.

sections.heading: Copyable template
sections.body: Fill in three processes.
sections.copyable:
Process 1: [PROCESS]. 3A band: Automate / Augment / Autonomize. Why (1 sentence): [REASON]. Human approval: [YES/NO + when].

Process 2: [PROCESS]. 3A band: … Why: … Human approval: …

Process 3: [PROCESS]. 3A band: … Why: … Human approval: …

sections.heading: Check
sections.body: Can you explain why at least one process is **not** in the Autonomize band (5 %) if you chose Automate or Augment? Can you name a process that **needs** a human? If not – go back to the diagram or example.

sections.heading: Where to apply
sections.body:
**Portfolio rule:** first inventory ~10 processes – keep most on rules (**Automate**); use agents only where the value clearly outweighs the cost of an error.

**Band rule:** need a sign-off or tone/fact approval → **Augment**; stable template and cheap errors → **Automate**; **Autonomize** – only with a limit, escalation and audit.

**Next step:** when a human must approve – slide **When does a human approve?**

content.footer: Next – slide 7: When does a human approve?

slides.title: When does a human approve?
slides.subtitle: Control mode by consequence and undo risk

sections.heading: In short
sections.body: Human control (industry term: **Human-in-the-loop / HITL**) is not a maturity ladder toward autopilot. It is **risk architecture**: the higher the consequence and the harder the action is to undo, the earlier a human must step in.

sections.heading: Do this now
sections.body: Pick a scenario and a control mode. The simulator shows whether the choice fits, what happens on error, and builds a rule for the “Minimal workflow brief.”

sections.heading: Check
sections.body: Can you name at least one process where result monitoring alone is **not enough**? Will your “Minimal workflow brief” human-approval line include mode, condition, escalation, and an audit record?

content.footer: Next – slide 9: Role and system prompt

slides.title: 5 workflow patterns for business
slides.subtitle: Chain, routing, parallel work, coordinator, evaluator

sections.heading: In short
sections.body: When one AI agent is no longer enough – pick a **workflow pattern** (not programming). Choose **one** – you will see a plan.

sections.heading: Do this now
sections.body: Pick **one** pattern for your process. After you choose, you will see only that pattern’s plan – copy it and fill it in. After the warm-up – orchestration walkthrough (HOW, not only the pattern).

toolChoiceBar.question: Which pattern will you apply to your process?

choices.label: Chain
choices.whenHint: **Yes:** steps run one after another. **No:** types differ or several work in parallel.

choices.label: Routing
choices.whenHint: **Yes:** different branch by type (complaint / inquiry). **No:** every case follows the same sequence.

choices.label: Parallel
choices.whenHint: **Yes:** several sources / specialists at once, then merge. **No:** the result depends on a prior step.

choices.label: Coordinator
choices.whenHint: **Yes:** you need to split sub-tasks dynamically. **No:** a fixed chain without assignment is enough.

choices.label: Generator + evaluator
choices.whenHint: **Yes:** draft + QC (email, FAQ, report). **No:** the quality risk is low – Agent (L1) is enough.

sections.heading: Copyable plan – Chain
sections.body: Copy and fill [DESCRIBE].
sections.copyable:
Process: [DESCRIBE]. Pattern: Chain.
List 3–5 steps in order (input → action → output).
For each step: who does it (human / AI / rule) and a done criterion.
Mark human approval on risky steps.

sections.heading: Copyable plan – Routing
sections.body: Copy and fill [DESCRIBE].
sections.copyable:
Process: [DESCRIBE]. Pattern: Routing.
Input types: [e.g. complaint / inquiry / proposal].
For each branch: who runs it, what output, when to escalate to a human.
Done criterion for all branches.

sections.heading: Copyable plan – Parallel
sections.body: Copy and fill [DESCRIBE].
sections.copyable:
Process: [DESCRIBE]. Pattern: Parallel work.
Parallel streams (2–3): [e.g. CRM + email].
For each: input, output.
Merge rule: how they become one summary + who approves.

sections.heading: Copyable plan – Coordinator
sections.body: Copy and fill [DESCRIBE].
sections.copyable:
You are the coordinator. Task: [DESCRIBE].
Break it into 2–3 subtasks. For each assign a role (specialist / evaluator),
input, output and handoff rule (when to pass to the next role).
Present the plan as a numbered list.

sections.heading: Copyable plan – Generator + evaluator
sections.body: Copy and fill [DESCRIBE].
sections.copyable:
Process: [DESCRIBE]. Pattern: Generator + evaluator.
Generator: what it creates (draft) and which sources.
Evaluator: QC criteria (facts, tone, risk) and when to send back for fixes.
Human approval: [when YES / NO].

sections.heading: Check
sections.body: Does the plan have a clear **completion criterion**? Do risky steps have **human approval**?

sections.heading: When NOT to use multi-agent
sections.body: If the task has 1–2 steps – one agent (Agent) is enough. Patterns without an evaluator are risky for finance, support and public content.

slides.title: Quick check: workflow patterns
slides.subtitle: 3 questions about the chain, routing and evaluator patterns

questions.question: Which workflow pattern fits when one step must happen after another?
options: Only one question without a pattern
questions.explanation: A chain fits when one step clearly follows another: query → classification → draft → send.

questions.question: Which pattern fits when a request is routed by type?
questions.explanation: Routing directs a request by type or category: complaint, inquiry, proposal and similar.

questions.question: Which pattern is safest when you need a draft and a quality check?
options: Only a generator, without a check
questions.explanation: Generator + evaluator creates a draft first, then checks quality and returns it for fixes.

slides.title: Agent orchestration simulation
slides.subtitle: Router ≠ Orchestrator; Checker ≠ Evaluator; targeted retry

sections.heading: In short
sections.body: The orchestrator does not do specialist work itself – it owns the plan, state and fix loops. Three differences: **Router = WHERE**, **orchestrator = HOW**; **Checker** looks at format/sources, while the **Evaluator** decides Approve / Retry / Human; on error → **targeted** retry, not a full restart.

sections.heading: Simulation
sections.body: Scenario: RFP summary (5 points) – each point needs a citation from a trusted source. Walk the 6 macro steps in the diagram.
sections.imageAlt: Agent orchestration flow: input, router, orchestrator, specialists (Researcher, Writer, Checker), evaluator, result

sections.heading: Do this now
sections.body: Walk all 6 steps. On **Error and RETRY**, notice the **RETRY** loop – what returns to the orchestrator and why everything is not restarted.

sections.heading: Check
sections.body: In one sentence: how does the **router** (WHERE) differ from the **orchestrator** (HOW)? When does the evaluator say **Retry**, and when does it **hand the task to a human**?

sections.heading: Three differences (deeper)
sections.body:
**1. Router vs orchestrator** – the router classifies the request before execution; the orchestrator owns the plan, state and retries.

**2. Agents vs tools** – agents have a role and rules; tools (search, API) are what they call.

**3. Checker vs Evaluator** – Checker looks at format/sources; Evaluator decides Approve / Retry / Human.

slides.title: Closed learning loop
slides.subtitle: Rules, skills, action history, check and lessons

sections.heading: In short
sections.body: An agent does not only run a task. A good system stores action history, checks the result, pulls lessons from mistakes and updates rules or skills for next time.

sections.heading: Learning loop
sections.body: Execution and learning – two layers. Click a step in the diagram.

sections.heading: Two system layers
sections.body:
**Execution:** task → rules → roles → result.

**Learning:** action history → check → lessons → update. A mistake in one trial makes the next trial better.

sections.heading: Blocks simply
sections.body:
**Rules** – what AI does not do and when it asks a human.

**Skills** – reusable abilities (search, writing, checking).

**Action history** – task, steps, errors, notes.

**Check** – whether the result met the criteria.

**Lessons** – what failed, what to change.

**Update** – changed rule, prompt, skill or test.

sections.heading: Do this now
sections.body: After one small scenario, write one lesson: what failed, which rule or skill fixes it, where that fix will be used next time.

sections.heading: Copyable lesson template
sections.body: Use it after practice or after any agent trial.
sections.copyable:
Lesson after an agent trial:
1) What happened?
2) What was the cause?
3) What do I update: rule, prompt, skill or test?
4) How will I check next time?

sections.heading: Check
sections.body: A good lesson changes the next trial. If you only describe a fact (“it failed”) but do not change a rule, skill or test – the learning loop does not close.

slides.title: Where your app or agent runs
slides.subtitle: Choose where it runs and when it starts

preCopyCheckBlock.heading: Check
preCopyCheckBlock.question: Which sentence correctly separates n8n from Railway?
options: n8n runs the program 24/7; Railway arranges the flow
Both do the same thing – fast automation
n8n builds the flow; Railway runs the program or agent
Railway is only needed for Zapier tools
preCopyCheckBlock.explanation: n8n arranges the flow; Railway runs the program. Different layers – if you mix them up, go back to “In short”.

sections.heading: In short
sections.body: Separate two decisions: **hosting** is where your app or agent runs; **mode** is when it starts work. If you only use Zapier or Make as a cloud service, the platform usually provides hosting for you.

sections.heading: Four layers
sections.body: First separate **what** you are choosing – not only the product name.

rows: How does data move between systems?
How do you click the UI when there is no API?
Where does the program run continuously (24/7)?

sections.heading: Where to host (orientation)
sections.body: Three common choices (no prices). Open this only when you run your own app.

rows: API + database + agent for a fast start
Simple web app and background worker
When you need to be near users in different countries

sections.heading: Do this now
sections.body: First decide whether you need separate hosting at all. Then pick **one operating mode** and copy only its template.

choices.label: Always-on
choices.whenHint: **Yes:** must listen for events in real time. **No:** a schedule is enough. E.g. Telegram / Discord bot.

choices.label: On a schedule (cron)
choices.whenHint: **Yes:** repeats on a schedule. **No:** must listen for messages continuously. E.g. price check in the morning.

choices.label: Webhook + background worker
choices.whenHint: **Yes:** a webhook starts a long background task. **No:** a short two- or three-step flow with no wait. E.g. PDF analysis, report.

Why (1 sentence): [ ]

sections.heading: More: hybrid and mistakes
sections.body:
**Hybrid:** form → n8n → AI agent → PostgreSQL → email; agent, API and DB run on hosting (e.g. Railway).

**Avoid:** (1) an AI agent where Zapier is enough; (2) RPA when an API exists; (3) serverless-only for a Discord bot – you need always-on.

**Optional in the template:** RPA yes/no; code – GitHub / local / none.

**Code:** if you write a program – see the optional slide **GitHub as a code source**.

content.footer: Next – slide 25: GitHub as a code source

slides.title: GitHub as a code source
slides.subtitle: Does your process need custom code?

sections.heading: In short
sections.body: **GitHub** stores code and its versions. A **platform as a service (PaaS)**, such as Railway or Render, runs that code online. If your whole process lives in Zapier or Make, you usually do not need GitHub.

sections.heading: When to use what – platforms
sections.body: Different places – different jobs.

rows: Backend, API, bots, AI agents, databases

sections.heading: Do this now
sections.body: Choose Yes or No. Base the decision on whether your process needs a custom app, API, or bot.

toolChoiceBar.question: Does your process need custom code?

choices.label: No – the platform is enough
choices.whenHint: **Example:** Zapier or Make handles form → CRM → email. The platform stores and runs the flow.

choices.label: Yes – I have an app or bot
choices.whenHint: **Example:** a Telegram bot stores its code on GitHub, while Railway runs it continuously.

sections.heading: Two contrasting examples
sections.body:
**No custom code:** Zapier receives a form, updates the CRM, and sends an email – no GitHub needed.

**Custom code:** a bot processes messages using your program – GitHub stores the code and a hosting platform runs it.

sections.heading: Copyable template
sections.body: Fill in your decision and get a short check.
sections.copyable:
Process: [PROCESS]
Do I have a custom app, API, or bot: [YES / NO]
Choice: [ZAPIER / MAKE IS ENOUGH | GITHUB + HOSTING NEEDED]
Hosting: [RAILWAY / RENDER / VERCEL / NOT NEEDED]
Why (1 sentence): [ ]

Check my choice in 3 lines. If it is too complex, suggest a simpler path.

sections.heading: Check
sections.body: Can you separate **“stores code”** (GitHub) from **“runs it”** (Railway / Render)? If not – go back to “In short”.

sections.heading: More: typical flow and mistakes
sections.body:
**Flow in one line:** local → commit/push → GitHub → auto-deploy → PaaS.

**Commands (if you already use git):** add → commit → push.

**Replit** – a fast prototype; not the same as production Railway / Render.

**Avoid:** keeping code only on your machine when you need reliable hosting or teamwork.

slides.title: Minimal workflow brief
slides.subtitle: 1-page outline + 3 tests + when a human approves

sections.heading: In short
sections.body: Before Module 12 practice, prepare a one-page workflow brief: the flow itself, three tests, and a rule for when a human decides. You will check this same artifact on the next slide and reuse it in practice.

sections.heading: Minimal brief
sections.body:
**A. Flow:** trigger, required input, condition if needed, 3–5 actions, result, and failure path.

**B. Three tests:** a success path, a missing field, and an unavailable or duplicate system event.

**C. Human decision:** when to stop, who approves, and what to record.

**Mini example:** form submitted → email validated → CRM record → email; if the email address is missing, stop and ask for that field.

sections.heading: Do this now
sections.body: Copy one template and fill it with your process. The quality evaluator in the next step will point to one place worth fixing.

sections.heading: Copyable template
sections.body: One page that you can hand to a colleague or an evaluator.
sections.copyable:
Minimal workflow brief

A. FLOW
Trigger: [WHAT STARTS IT]
Required input: [FIELDS]
Condition, if needed: [RULE]
Actions (3–5): [1] → [2] → [3]
Result: [WHAT IS CREATED AND WHERE]
If it fails: [STOP / RETRY / NOTIFY]

B. TESTS
1) Success path: [INPUT → EXPECTED RESULT]
2) Missing field: [EXPECTED RESPONSE]
3) System unavailable or duplicate: [WHAT TO DO]

C. HUMAN DECISION
When to send to a human: [CONDITION]
Who approves: [ROLE]
What to record: [TIME, DECISION, RESULT]

sections.heading: Check
sections.body: Do you have all three parts: **A – flow, B – three tests, C – human decision**? From this page, could a colleague understand what happens and what to do on failure?
